title: A Rule You Can Say
bigQuestion: How do a painted line and a short written rule help strangers play one game?

story.title: One Line, Two Classes
story.kicker: Two children from different classes meet at a painted line, and both know what it means.
paragraphs: Two classes come out to the blacktop at the same time. Maya is in first grade. Leo is in second grade. They have never met before today.
A long white line is painted across the blacktop. Maya stops behind it. Leo stops behind it too. Nobody told either of them to wait there.
"Everybody starts behind the line," Maya says. Leo nods. He learned the same rule last year. The paint said it before either of them spoke.
Grown-up games grew the same way. Long ago, people wrote their rules down and marked lines on fields. Then strangers from far-away towns could play together.
story.think: What is one rule at your school that fits in one short sentence?

lessons.title: A Stone Line at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: At Olympia in Greece, a stone starting line from ancient races is still in the ground.
reading: Olympia is a very old place for games in Greece. Greek tradition says the first race there was in 776 BCE. It was one length of the track.
Runners began at a *starting line* made of stone. That stone line is still in the ground today. Visitors can walk up and see it.
Only men and boys could race in these games. Girls had their own race there, a Greek writer said. It honored the goddess Hera.

words.d: a line where a race begins

look.title: A Line Made of Stone
look.text: Picture a long strip of pale stone set in the dirt. It has lasted more than 2,000 years. Runners from many Greek cities stood at this same line. None of them needed a book to know where to begin.
look.prompt: Why might a line made of stone work better than one scratched in dirt?

check.q: What is still in the ground at Olympia?
check.why: The ancient stone starting line can still be seen at Olympia.

check.q: Who could race in the old Olympic games?
check.why: Only men and boys raced in those games.

check.q: Which year does Greek tradition give for the first race?
check.why: Greek tradition dates the first race at Olympia to 776 BCE.

lessons.title: Games With No Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Old town football games in England had few rules and no painted lines.
reading: Long ago, many English towns played a rough ball game on holidays. Hundreds of people joined in. There were no painted lines at all.
In 1314, a London order said no football in the city streets. It said the game made too much noise. This kind of order is a *ban*.
One English town, Ashbourne, still plays this old game each year. Its two goals are about three miles apart.

words.d: a rule that says something is not allowed

look.title: London Says No
look.text: The London order said there was great noise in the city from crowds chasing large balls. It said this game must stop inside the city.
look.cite: Proclamation for the City of London, issued in the name of King Edward II, 1314
look.prompt: What problem did the London order name?

check.q: When did London ban football in its streets?
check.why: The London order came in 1314.

check.q: What is a ban?
choices: a rule that says something is not allowed
check.why: A ban says something is not allowed.

check.q: How far apart are the goals at Ashbourne?
check.why: The Ashbourne goals are about three miles apart.

lessons.title: The Knickerbockers Write Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In 1845, the Knickerbocker club of New York wrote down 20 rules for baseball.
reading: In 1845, a *club* in New York City wrote rules for baseball. It was the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club. Its list had 20 rules.
In 1846, the Knickerbockers played a game in Hoboken, New Jersey. The field was called the Elysian Fields.
A story says Abner Doubleday invented baseball in 1839. A report in 1907 said so. Historians found no proof. It is a *legend*.

words.d: a group of people who meet to play a game together
an old story many people tell that may not be true

look.title: Story or Record?
look.text: Card one says: A man named Doubleday made up baseball in 1839. No paper from 1839 backs it up. Card two says: A New York club wrote 20 rules in 1845. Those rules were written down that year.
look.prompt: Which card can historians check? Why?

check.q: How many rules did the Knickerbockers write?
check.why: The Knickerbocker list of 1845 had 20 rules.

check.q: What do historians say about the Doubleday story?
choices: it is a legend with no proof
check.why: Historians found no proof. The Doubleday story is a legend.

check.q: Where did the Knickerbockers play in 1846?
check.why: They played at the Elysian Fields in Hoboken, New Jersey.

lessons.title: A Meeting in London, 1863
lessons.mainIdea: On 26 October 1863, football clubs met in London and formed the Football Association.
reading: In the 1800s, English schools played football in different ways. Each school had its own rules. So two schools could not easily play each other.
On 26 October 1863, club leaders met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They started the *Football Association*. A lawyer named Ebenezer Morley helped lead it.
In December 1863, the group agreed on 13 laws. That game grew into the one Americans call soccer.

words.d: the group formed in London in 1863 to write one set of football rules

look.title: The First Laws
look.text: The first laws of the Football Association, agreed in December 1863, said how big the field could be. They also said how the goals should be marked and how a game begins.
look.cite: The Football Association, Laws of the Game, December 1863
look.prompt: Why would the first laws talk about the size of the field?

check.q: Where did the clubs meet in 1863?
check.why: They met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863.

check.q: How many laws did the group agree on in December 1863?
check.why: The Football Association agreed on 13 laws in December 1863.

check.q: Why was a shared rule book needed?
choices: each school played with its own rules
check.why: Each school had its own rules, so schools could not easily play each other.

lessons.title: Naismith Pins Up 13 Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith wrote 13 rules for basketball and pinned them up in the Springfield gym.
reading: Naismith wrote 13 *rules* for his new game. They fit on two typed pages. He pinned the pages up in the gym at Springfield.
In January 1892, the school paper printed the rules. Other YMCA gyms read them. Soon the game spread to many cities.
In 2010, the two pages were sold for about 4.3 million dollars. Today they are kept at the University of Kansas, where Naismith later taught.

words.d: written words that say what players may and may not do

look.title: Pages on a Wall
look.text: Picture two typed pages pinned to a gym wall in 1891. A young man reads them before class. He has never played this game. The pages tell him what is allowed.
look.prompt: How do written rules help someone who is new to a game?

check.why: The school paper printed the rules in January 1892.

lessons.title: From Hourglass to Rectangle
lessons.mainIdea: The first lawn tennis court was shaped like an hourglass, but by 1877 courts were rectangles.
reading: In 1873, Walter Wingfield showed a new lawn game in England. In 1874, he got a *patent* for it. A patent is a paper that says an idea is yours.
His court was shaped like an hourglass. It was narrow at the net and wide at the back.
In 1877, the All England Club held a tennis contest at Wimbledon. Its court was a rectangle. Tennis courts are still rectangles today.

words.d: a government paper that says an idea or invention belongs to you

look.title: How Long Is Each Court?
look.cite: FIVB, ITF and NFHS rule books; NBA Official Rules
look.prompt: Which court is the longest? Which is the shortest?

check.q: What shape was Wingfield's first court?
check.why: Wingfield's court was narrow at the net and wide at the back, like an hourglass.

check.q: What is a patent?
choices: a paper that says an idea is yours
check.why: A patent says an invention belongs to the person who made it.

check.q: What shape was the court at Wimbledon in 1877?
check.why: The 1877 Wimbledon court was a rectangle, like courts today.

lessons.title: One Book for the World's Fields
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886, a board called IFAB has kept soccer's Laws of the Game.
reading: In 1886, football groups from England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland formed a board. It is called IFAB. It keeps soccer's *Laws of the Game*.
FIFA joined IFAB in 1913. Today the Laws of the Game has 17 laws. Law 1 is about the field and its lines.
Law 1 says every line must be the same width. No line may be wider than 5 inches. A field in Chicago and a field in Brazil follow the same law.

words.d: the rule book for soccer, kept by IFAB
the International Football Association Board, which keeps soccer's rules

look.title: Law 1
look.text: The field of play must be a rectangle marked with lines. All lines must be the same width, no wider than 12 cm (5 inches).
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 1: The Field of Play
look.prompt: Why might every field in the world need the same kind of lines?

check.q: When was IFAB formed?
check.why: Four British football groups formed IFAB in 1886.

check.q: How many laws are in the Laws of the Game today?
check.why: Today the Laws of the Game has 17 laws.

check.q: What is Law 1 about?
check.why: Law 1 is about the field of play and its lines.

lessons.title: The IHSA Handbook
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1900, the IHSA has kept one set of rules for Illinois high school sports.
reading: The *IHSA* began in 1900. The letters stand for Illinois High School Association. Its office is in Bloomington, Illinois.
Member schools agree to follow the same *by-laws*. By-laws are written rules a group agrees to. They say who may play and how state contests work.
The IHSA crowned its first boys tennis champion in 1912. Boys wrestling began in 1937. The first girls wrestling state finals came in 2022.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, begun in 1900
written rules that members of a group agree to follow

check.why: The first girls wrestling state finals came in 2022.
